opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the more important questions for figuring out timelines. The basic picture is: right now a lot of the progress we're seeing comes from doing RL on tasks where you can check the answer, like competition math, coding problems with test cases, and increasingly more agentic software engineering tasks. A natural worry is that this only gets you strong performance in narrow, easily verifiable domains, and that the messy, hard-to-check parts of running an AI company won't be covered.

My view is that you might get surprisingly far even if transfer is fairly weak. If you look at what an AI company actually does, a huge fraction of the labor is software engineering and ML research engineering: writing training infrastructure, debugging distributed systems, running experiments, analyzing results, optimizing kernels. A lot of that is quite verifiable, or at least can be made verifiable with some effort. Did the code pass the tests? Did the run go faster? Did the loss go down? Did this ablation reproduce? So companies can potentially build RL environments that directly target much of the work they care about, rather than hoping a model trained on math puzzles somehow generalizes to research taste.

Where it gets harder is the less checkable stuff: picking which research directions are promising, judging whether an experiment was actually informative, high-level prioritization, noticing that you're fooling yourself. Those have long feedback loops and noisy signals. Here I think it's an open question. You might be able to get partway via proxies, like training on whether an idea's predicted outcome matched the actual outcome, or using human or AI judges, but those proxies are exploitable, and you risk getting models that look good to graders rather than actually being good.

So my rough guess is that you could plausibly get to the point where AIs are doing most of the engineering work at an AI company, which would already be a big speedup, maybe a large multiplier on progress, without needing much transfer. Getting to full automation, where the AIs are also doing the research direction-setting well, probably either needs better transfer than we've clearly seen, or a lot of clever work building feedback signals for those fuzzier skills. And of course, once you've automated much of the engineering, you can throw a lot more AI labor at building those environments, so there's a feedback loop that could make the remaining gap close faster than you'd naively expect.

I'd put meaningful probability on that path working, which is part of why I don't think "RL doesn't generalize much" should make people very confident timelines are long.

r001.rationale: The response says AIs could plausibly do most engineering work at an AI company through targeted RL, without needing much transfer.

r002.rationale: It mentions predicting an idea’s outcome as a possible proxy, but does not identify outcome prediction as a substantial component of research taste.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose transferring forecasting ability from smaller ML projects to larger ones.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest generating many research ideas and choosing among them by predicted outcomes.

r005.rationale: It contrasts verifiable engineering work with research direction-setting and prioritization, noting that the latter have long, noisy feedback loops that make them harder to automate.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's actually a pretty interesting question here, which is: how much of the work of an AI company can you just directly train on with RL, where you set up the task, you have some reward signal, and you just grind on it?

And my view is that a surprisingly large fraction of the work is at least somewhat amenable to this. Like, a lot of what goes on at an AI company is writing code, running experiments, looking at the results, deciding what to do next. And for the coding part, you can pretty clearly set up RL environments. You've got tests, you've got whether the code works, whether the pull request gets merged, that sort of thing. For the experiment-running part, it's a bit harder, but you can imagine setting up environments where the model has to improve some metric on some small-scale version of the problem, and you reward it based on how much it improves the metric. And that's actually a fairly clean signal.

So the picture would be something like: you don't need the model to be generally good at everything, you don't need huge amounts of transfer from domains that are totally unrelated. You just need to directly train on the thing you care about, which is "do ML research and engineering," and the AI companies are in a pretty unusual position here because they are themselves the customer. They know exactly what tasks they want automated, they have a lot of in-house data about what good work looks like, and they can construct environments that look a lot like the actual job.

Now, I do think there are caveats. One is that some of the work is pretty long-horizon and the feedback is sparse. Like, if a research direction takes three months to pan out, that's a hard thing to do RL on directly. You'd want to break it into pieces, or find proxies, and the proxies might not be great. Another is that there's a bunch of taste and judgment involved, like "which of these ten experiments is actually worth running," and that's a thing where you might need either a lot of transfer from general capability, or you need some way to get a reward signal on taste, which is harder.

But my overall guess is that even with relatively limited transfer, you could get pretty far. Maybe the first 50 or 70 percent of the way toward automating the labor at an AI company, at least the more junior and mid-level research engineering work, is reachable just by directly doing RL on things that look like that work. And then the question of whether you get the rest is partly a question of whether the capabilities you build up from doing that somehow generalize to the harder, more open-ended, more judgment-heavy stuff. And I'm genuinely uncertain about that. I think it's plausible that it does generalize a fair amount, because a lot of what "research taste" is, is just having seen a lot of things work and not work, and RL on a huge number of smaller tasks might give you a version of that.

So I'd say: RL gets you a lot, probably more than people's intuitions from a few years ago would have suggested. But the last stretch, the part where you've fully replaced the senior researchers, is where I'd put most of my uncertainty, and that's where I think transfer and generalization start mattering more.

r001.rationale: The response says direct RL could cover roughly 50–70% of the work, while full automation of senior research remains uncertain and may depend more on transfer and generalization.

r002.rationale: It mentions judgment about which experiments are worth running, but does not identify predicting experimental outcomes as a substantial part of research taste.

r003.rationale: It discusses small-scale task environments and possible generalization, but does not propose transferring forecasting ability from smaller ML projects to larger ones.

r004.rationale: It mentions choosing among experiments, but not generating many research ideas and selecting them based on predicted outcomes as a substitute for insight-driven selection.

r005.rationale: It cites long research timelines and sparse feedback as challenges, but does not compare them with strategic CEO decision-making or say that such decisions are harder to automate than AI R&D.

astra-6.text:
I think it could go pretty far, because you can train on tasks that are very close to the work you actually want the system to do. If you want it to run machine learning experiments, you can have it run machine learning experiments and reward it for getting better results. You don’t necessarily need it to learn some very general skill in a different domain and then transfer that into AI research.

The harder question is how long a feedback loop you can handle. There’s a big difference between improving a particular piece of code, where you can quickly check whether it works, and deciding what research direction the company should pursue over the next six months. In the latter case, it’s much harder to get enough training examples and to tell whether a decision was actually good or just lucky.

So I’d expect a substantial amount of the work to be amenable to fairly direct training, especially the work with short, measurable feedback loops. You could then have humans providing the high-level direction while the systems do more and more of the execution. Whether that gets you all the way to an automated company is less clear, but you could get a lot of acceleration without solving that last part.

r001.rationale: The response says direct training could handle substantial work and provide acceleration, but it does not claim that research engineering could be nearly fully automated.

r002.rationale: It discusses difficulty evaluating long-term decisions, but does not identify outcome prediction as a component of research taste.

r003.rationale: It gives no proposal to transfer forecasting ability from smaller ML projects to larger ones.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest generating many research ideas and ranking them by predicted outcomes as a substitute for insight-driven selection.

r005.rationale: It contrasts quickly checking code changes with choosing a research direction over six months, noting that longer feedback makes examples scarce and evaluation harder.

sol-6.1.text:
I think potentially quite far, though it depends on what you mean by automating an AI company. If you mean doing the research and engineering required to build better AI systems, a lot of that work has feedback you could in principle train on. You make a change, run an experiment, and see whether the resulting model is better or whether you can get the same performance more cheaply.

So you could imagine reinforcement learning directly on fairly substantial chunks of that process. And then you don’t necessarily need the model to learn something in one domain and generalise it to AI research. You’re training it to do AI research.

The big uncertainty is how well this works as the tasks get longer and the feedback gets more expensive. There’s a substantial difference between improving something where you can run a quick experiment and choosing a research direction that takes months to evaluate. You might also get systems that are very good at optimising whatever your training setup measures, but miss important things outside that setup.

But I wouldn’t be comfortable assuming those difficulties prevent you from automating most of the relevant work. You could have a system that’s relatively specialised, that isn’t able to replace humans across the economy, but that can nevertheless do a large fraction of the work involved in developing the next generation of AI.

r001.rationale: It says reinforcement learning could automate “most” of the relevant AI development work, including substantial chunks of research and engineering, without requiring cross-domain generalization.

r002.rationale: It discusses evaluating experiments, but does not identify outcome prediction as a substantial component of research taste.

r003.rationale: It does not propose transferring forecasting ability from smaller ML projects to larger ones.

r004.rationale: It does not describe generating many research ideas and selecting among them based on predicted outcomes.

r005.rationale: It contrasts quick experimental feedback with research directions that take months to evaluate, presenting slower feedback as a difficulty for automating that work compared with faster AI development tasks.
